title: Network Exploration and Diagnostics
description: Use CMD and PowerShell network commands to investigate your network infrastructure
objective: Students will use network diagnostic commands to map their network, test connectivity, trace routes, perform DNS lookups, and identify active connections

steps.title: Find Your Network Identity
steps.instructions:
Open **Command Prompt** (search 'cmd').

```cmd
ipconfig /all
```

Find and write down these values:
- **IPv4 Address** (e.g., 192.168.1.105)
- **Subnet Mask** (e.g., 255.255.255.0)
- **Default Gateway** (e.g., 192.168.1.1 — this is your router)
- **DNS Servers** (e.g., 8.8.8.8)
- **DHCP Enabled** (Yes/No)
- **Physical Address (MAC)** (e.g., A4-83-E7-2B-FF-01)

Now find your **public IP** (the IP the world sees):
```cmd
curl ifconfig.me
```

Notice: Your private IP (192.168.x.x) and public IP are different. Why? Because of NAT (Network Address Translation) — your router translates between them.

steps.title: Test Connectivity
steps.instructions:
```cmd
:: Test 1: Can you reach the internet?
ping 8.8.8.8
```
This pings Google's DNS server directly by IP. If this works → your internet connection is fine.

```cmd
:: Test 2: Can DNS resolve names?
ping google.com
```
If Test 1 works but Test 2 fails → DNS is the problem.

```cmd
:: Test 3: Can you reach your router?
ping 192.168.1.1
```
Replace with your Default Gateway. If this fails → your WiFi/Ethernet connection is broken.

```cmd
:: Test 4: Speed comparison
ping -n 20 google.com
ping -n 20 8.8.8.8
```
Compare average response times. DNS adds a small delay.

Document: Which test gives the fastest response? Which is slowest?

steps.title: Trace the Route
steps.instructions:
```cmd
tracert google.com
```

This shows every router (hop) between your PC and Google's server.

Each line shows:
```
Hop#  Time1  Time2  Time3  RouterIP/Name
  1    1ms    1ms    1ms   192.168.1.1      ← Your router
  2    5ms    4ms    5ms   10.0.0.1         ← ISP's first router
  3   12ms   11ms   12ms  ...               ← ISP network
  ...
  12   35ms   34ms   36ms  142.250.77.110   ← Google's server
```

Questions to answer:
1. How many hops to reach Google?
2. Which hop has the highest delay? (This is a bottleneck)
3. Are any hops showing `* * *` (request timed out)? That router blocks traceroute — it's normal.

Now try:
```cmd
tracert techpath.biz
```
Compare the number of hops.

steps.title: DNS Investigation
steps.instructions:
```cmd
:: Look up IP address of a domain
nslookup google.com

:: Look up using Google's DNS specifically
nslookup google.com 8.8.8.8

:: Look up TechPath
nslookup techpath.biz

:: Look up mail server records
nslookup -type=mx gmail.com
```

Notice how some domains return multiple IP addresses — this is load balancing (multiple servers handle requests).

Now test DNS speed:
```cmd
:: Flush DNS cache first
ipconfig /flushdns

:: Time a DNS lookup
nslookup google.com
```
The first lookup is slightly slower (not cached). The second lookup is faster (cached).

steps.title: Active Connections
steps.instructions:
```cmd
:: Show all active network connections
netstat -an
```

This shows:
- **Local Address** (your IP:port)
- **Foreign Address** (server IP:port)
- **State** (ESTABLISHED, LISTENING, TIME_WAIT)

Filter for specific info:
```cmd
:: Only established connections
netstat -an | findstr ESTABLISHED

:: Connections on port 443 (HTTPS)
netstat -an | findstr :443

:: Find which program is using a connection
netstat -ano | findstr ESTABLISHED
```
The last column shows PID. Find this PID in Task Manager → Details tab to see which app.

Count your established connections. Each one is an active communication channel — browsers have many because each tab/request is separate.

**Document all findings in your lab report with screenshots.**

expected_output: A report containing ipconfig output with key values identified, ping results with analysis, traceroute output with hop analysis, DNS lookup results for multiple domains, and netstat connection count with app identification
